newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai copper futures end up on short-covering.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai copper futures end up on short-covering.

text.p: Shanghai copper futures ended up on Monday with most contracts near their intraday highs due to short-covering after copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) held its ground above $2,400 on Friday, traders said.
The most actively traded October 1997 contract ended at 21,590 yuan ($2,604) per tonne, up 200 yuan. It opened at 21,450 yuan, hitting a low of 21,400 and a high of 21,610 yuan.
July rose 190 to 21,290 yuan, August 240 to 21,450, September 220 to 21,500, November 190 to 21,580 and December 200 to 21,600.
Combined volume fell to 62,930 tonnes from 96,550 tonnes.
Copper opened higher and rose further for most of the session.

Traders said Friday's LME gains triggered short-covering on the Shanghai market but investors were not optimistic about the future trend as the LME would continue to focus on July date tightness in the short term.
"Investors were seen covering their short positions for heavy profits after sharp falls over the past few trading days," one trader said.
Most contracts have fallen nearly 1,000 yuan per tonne during last week due to panic selling.
"But today's gains can not change weak market sentiment and the bearish market trend in the long run," the trader said.
Spot copper prices are around 21,350-21,400 yuan in the Shanghai area, up from the 21,200-21,300 yuan level late last week due to a rebound on the futures market.
Traders said technical charts showed copper was still in a downward channel and would meet strong selling pressure at high levels.
"Most buying today was for quick profits and some investors are waiting for copper to rise in order to build short positions at higher levels," a second trader said.
Aluminium ended down. July fell 130 to 13,590 yuan per tonne, August 180 to 13,650, September 20 to 13,880, October was unchanged at 14,000 and November fell 180 to 14,000 yuan per tonne.
Combined volume fell to 1,680 tonnes from 2,160 tonnes.
